abstract: In this edition, we highlight several important developments across the Huntington's disease therapeutic pipeline. We discuss the launch and subsequent discontinuation of POINT-HD, the first-in-human phase I study of RG6496 (Hoffmann-La Roche), an allele-selective antisense oligonucleotide designed to selectively lower mutant huntingtin while largely preserving wild-type huntingtin expression. We also discuss the launch of two phase III efficacy trials: INVEST-HD, evaluating votoplam (Novartis Pharmaceuticals), and PRECISE-HD, evaluating pridopidine (Prilenia). In addition, we summarise recent advances across the field, including preclinical updates for LQT-23 (LoQus23), SRP-1005 (Sarepta Therapeutics) and HRN001 (Harness Therapeutics); interim 12-month clinical results from SKY-0515 (Skyhawk Therapeutics); the announcement by uniQure that 3-year data from the phase I/II AMT-130 study may support a Biologics License Application seeking accelerated approval and Roche's discontinuation of the phase II GENERATION HD2 study of tominersen. Finally, we provide an updated listing of registered and ongoing clinical trials in Huntington's disease.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypertension remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, yet current therapeutic strategies lack sustained efficacy and long-term stability. Our study aimed to construct a humanized rodent model for drugs development especially currently prevalent small interfering RNA medication.
METHODS: A humanized hypertensive mouse model was generated by subcutaneous injection of neonatal mice with adeno-associated viruses encoding hAGT (human angiotensinogen) and hRENIN (human renin). Blood pressure was monitored weekly via tail-cuff plethysmography. Expression of hAGT and hRENIN was assessed by ELISA, Western blot, and reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Cardiac function was evaluated by echocardiography at 4 and 6 months postinjection. Hypertension-associated comorbidities were examined through histological analysis and ELISA. A modified N-acetylgalactosamine-conjugated small interfering RNA targeting human hepatic AGT (GalNAc-siAGT) was screened and subcutaneously administered to humanized hypertensive mice, either alone or in combination with valsartan, to evaluate therapeutic efficacy.
RESULTS: The dual adeno-associated virus-induced humanized hypertensive model exhibited a sustained hypertension for 6 months and manifested prevalent comorbidities, including heart failure and kidney disease. This modified GalNAc-siAGT demonstrated significant activity in knocking down hAGT both in vitro and in vivo. Only a single subcutaneous injection of GalNAc-siAGT in humanized hypertensive mice led to a sustained reduction in blood pressure lasting for 2 months, accompanied by cardio- and renoprotective effects. Moreover, combining GalNAc-siAGT with the renin-angiotensin system blocker, valsartan, significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy.
CONCLUSIONS: Our study validated the antihypertensive therapeutic effect of GalNAc-siAGT in a humanized hypertensive murine model while highlighting the translational potential of this model for clinical drug development.

abstract: CRISPR-Cas genome editing represents one of the most transformative advances in modern molecular biology, enabling programmable site-specific genetic modification that has revolutionized functional genomics and precision therapeutic development. Beyond canonical Cas9 nucleases, the CRISPR toolkit has diversified into precision base editors, prime editors, CRISPR-associated transposases, and Cas12/Cas13 RNA-targeting effectors, each with distinct mechanistic properties. Clinically, ex vivo CRISPR therapies for hemoglobinopathies have secured regulatory approval, while base editing, prime editing, and in vivo Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR)-T candidates are advancing through trials for a broad spectrum of hematologic, oncologic, and rare genetic disorders. However, existing reviews largely address technical innovation or clinical translation in isolation, lacking a holistic, up-to-date synthesis of the full bench-to-bedside trajectory of CRISPR technology. This review systematically dissects the molecular mechanisms, advantages, and limitations of core CRISPR editing platforms; summarizes pivotal clinical data across hemoglobinopathies, CAR-T immunotherapy, muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, cardiometabolic diseases and rare monogenic diseases; evaluates delivery systems including lipid nanoparticles and viral vectors; and discusses key translational barriers such as off-target genotoxicity and immunogenicity alongside emerging optimization strategies. This work provides a holistic bench-to-bedside framework for CRISPR research, offering critical insights to advance next-generation precision genetic medicine.

abstract: Advanced therapeutics, including programmable nucleic acid-based therapies (NATs), such as small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), CRISPR-Cas 9 editing systems, modified in vitro transcribed messenger RNAs (mRNAs) and Adeno-associated viruses (AAVs), have the potential to transform healthcare. However, while there have been considerable successes, there have also been notable clinical failures in early-stage human trials, which slowed down the progression of these therapeutic platforms. Multiple trials of NATs have been halted or discontinued, or approved products carry black box warnings as unforeseen or underestimated toxicities and poor efficacy have been observed in humans. There are a variety of reasons for failure of NATs, one of which is that many preclinical studies lack disease modelling in a human-relevant manner and, therefore, do not capture disease-specific effects on therapy tolerability and efficacy. This Perspective provides a short overview of why better human disease modelling is required to understand the potential therapeutic liabilities of NATs across modalities.

abstract: Gynecological cancers, including ovarian, cervical, and endometrial cancers, remain major contributors to female morbidity and mortality worldwide. Conventional treatments-surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy-have improved outcomes, but advanced or recurrent disease is still associated with poor prognosis, chemoresistance, and tumor heterogeneity. Immunotherapy has emerged as a transformative strategy because of its specificity and potential for durable responses. However, the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and inefficient delivery of immunotherapeutic agents limit clinical benefit. Nanocarriers, including organic, inorganic, and biomimetic platforms, can improve targeted delivery, sustained release, biocompatibility, and tumor microenvironment remodeling, thereby enhancing immunotherapy. This review summarizes major immunotherapeutic modalities for gynecological cancers-immune checkpoint blockade, CAR-T cell therapy, tumor vaccines, and oncolytic viruses-and the classification and characteristics of commonly used nanocarriers. We focus on nanocarrier-mediated immunotherapeutic mechanisms in ovarian, cervical, and endometrial cancers, and further highlight emerging lipid nanoparticle/mRNA and programmable RNA delivery strategies. Finally, we analyze challenges in clinical translation and provide perspectives for future development, aiming to support fundamental research and clinical application of nano-immunotherapy in gynecological malignancies.

abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a shared mechanism across neurological disease. Specifically, impaired oxidative phosphorylation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial DNA damage are factors in primary mitochondrial disorders and major neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson, Alzheimer, and Huntington diseases, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. This review surveys the mechanisms driving mitochondrial dysfunction and evaluates the current landscape of gene-editing technologies developed to address them. We examine mitochondria-targeted editors and nuclear-targeted editors, examining the editing capability, delivery constraints, and off-target risk of each. Heteroplasmy-shifting nucleases currently offer the strongest in vivo evidence for mtDNA-directed therapy, while base editors extend correction to homoplasmic mutations at the cost of a narrower editing scope and off-target editing. Nuclear editing platforms avoid the mitochondrial gRNA import barrier entirely, allowing current technologies to achieve the most progress toward functional, behavioral rescue in animal models. Across all platforms, delivery efficiency, off-target specificity, and translation from rodent to primate models remain unresolved barriers to clinical application. Gene editing for mitochondrial dysfunction is highly creditable as a precision therapy for genetically defined disease subsets, including primary mitochondrial disease and other neurodegenerative disorders with a known nuclear driver, rather than as a universal strategy for sporadic neurodegeneration, where mitochondrial dysfunction arises from multifactorial and poorly localized causes.

abstract: Viral diseases remain a major global health challenge despite substantial advances in vaccination, antiviral therapeutics, and public-health interventions. However, current antiviral strategies are still constrained by important gaps, including rapid viral evolution, limited broad-spectrum efficacy, immune escape, antiviral resistance, incomplete durability of protection, and inequitable global access to prevention and treatment. This review provides a comprehensive and integrated overview of contemporary antiviral prevention and therapeutic strategies, spanning vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, direct-acting antivirals, host-targeted therapies, immunomodulators, RNA-based therapeutics, gene-editing technologies, and cellular immunotherapies. We discuss the mechanistic foundations, clinical applications, pharmacologic considerations, and translational challenges associated with each modality across major human viral pathogens, including HIV, HBV, HCV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, RSV, Ebola virus, arboviruses, and herpesviruses. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging innovations such as long-acting prophylaxis, Fc-engineered monoclonal antibodies, nanoparticle and mucosal vaccine platforms, CRISPR-based antiviral systems, and broadly protective host-directed approaches designed to overcome resistance and enhance pandemic preparedness. In addition, we highlight the growing importance of real-time genomic surveillance and equitable global deployment strategies in shaping future antiviral responses, collectively underscoring that the next generation of antiviral medicine will depend on the convergence of universal immunization strategies, durable therapeutics, precision immune modulation, and rapidly deployable platform technologies capable of addressing both endemic and emerging viral threats.

title: Therapeutic and Prophylactic Agents for Viral Diseases: Current Status, Challenges, and Future Prospects.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive breast cancer subtype characterized by high metastatic potential and limited targeted therapeutic options. Lipocalin-2 (LCN2) has been implicated in tumor progression and metastatic dissemination, but its functional role in TNBC remains incompletely understood. This study investigated the role of LCN2 in the human TNBC cell line MDA-MB-231.
METHODS: Stable LCN2-deficient (LCN2KO) cells were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, followed by isolation of single-cell-derived clones. RNA sequencing was performed to characterize transcriptomic changes, with selected findings validated by reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR). Western blotting was used to assess protein-level changes. Transwell migration and invasion assays and adhesion assays were performed to evaluate functional effects.
RESULTS: LCN2KO cells largely retained the mesenchymal phenotype of parental cells. RNA sequencing revealed changes associated with inflammatory signaling, iron homeostasis, oxidative stress, ferroptosis-related processes, and cellular metabolism. Functional assays demonstrated reduced migration, invasion, and adhesion, accompanied by altered adhesion to extracellular matrix components.
DISCUSSION: LCN2 deficiency is associated with transcriptional and functional changes in MDA-MB-231 cells, particularly affecting migratory and invasive behavior and cell-matrix interactions, while largely preserving the mesenchymal phenotype. These findings provide further insight into the role of LCN2 in cellular processes relevant to TNBC progression and metastatic behavior.

title: Comprehensive characterization of the cellular and molecular consequences of LCN2 loss in MDA-MB-231 triple-negative breast cancer cells.

abstract: Breast cancer progression is driven by molecular heterogeneity, drug resistance (DR), and interactions within the tumour microenvironment (TME), creating an urgent need for therapies that can selectively suppress disease-associated genes. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) can silence targets involved in tumour growth, treatment resistance, and immune evasion. Its therapeutic potential, however, depends on overcoming rapid degradation and clearance, limited tumour accumulation, poor cellular uptake, and endosomal entrapment. Lipid-based and polymer-mediated delivery systems (DS) protect siRNA and facilitate its transport, while chemical modifications, molecular conjugates, and physical delivery methods offer additional ways to improve stability or access to target cells. In BC models, these strategies have been investigated for targeted therapy, reversal of DR, and modulation of the TME to support antitumor immunity. Despite encouraging preclinical findings, effective tumour delivery, sustained gene silencing, off-target effects, and immune activation remain significant barriers to clinical translation. This review brings together advances in siRNA delivery and their applications against BC progression, DR, and immune evasion, while defining the barriers that must be overcome to translate effective gene silencing into meaningful clinical benefit.

abstract:
This is an open-label, single-arm, single-site Phase I trial in a total of 20 healthy participants at GARM Próspera, Roatán, Honduras. Each participant receives one intravenous administration of 0.5 mg AKL003 on Day 0.

Screening is followed by one treatment visit at GARM Próspera covering Day -1 to Day 2. Scheduled follow-up comprises Day 7 and the actual remote Final Visit (nominal Day 28 ±7 days), following local assessments under Investigator oversight.

Safety is assessed through adverse events, clinical examinations, vital signs, ECG and laboratory testing. Six months of passive safety follow-up after the individual Final Visit or Early Termination Visit.

PsyTool, QoL, Oura and DNA methylation assessments are retained. Exploratory changes do not establish clinical efficacy without a concurrent control group.
description:
This is an open-label, single-arm, single-site Phase I trial evaluating safety, tolerability and serum alpha-Klotho protein expression after a single intravenous administration of AKL003, a proprietary alpha-Klotho mRNA formulated in lipid nanoparticles. Twenty participants in total will receive AKL003 at GARM Próspera, Roatán, Honduras.

Each participant will receive one 0.5 mg intravenous administration on Day 0. Screening and later laboratory follow-up may be conducted through designated providers in the USA under the responsible Investigator's oversight. One treatment visit at GARM Próspera, Roatán, Honduras is required, covering Day -1 through Day 2. Scheduled follow-up comprises Day 7 and the actual remote Final Visit (nominal Day 28 ±7 days), following local laboratory and physical assessments. All participants follow the protocol-defined eligibility criteria, dose, pre- and post-treatment dexamethasone regimen, assessment schedule and safety procedures.

Systemic reactogenicity events, including fever, headache, myalgia, fatigue, nausea/vomiting, diarrhea and increased heart rate, will be assessed as adverse events. Severity will be graded ; CRS will be graded according to ASTCT criteria where applicable.

All participants will be informed about potential clinical activity and reactogenicity, which may be influenced by increased aKL serum levels or the lipid nanoparticle formulation. Participants will be instructed to contact the trial site to schedule an on-site visit in case of any unexpected adverse event (unscheduled visit,). All such occurrences will be documented as part of the drug candidate's safety evaluation.

Participants will use an electronic diary for daily symptoms through Day 7 and report new or worsening symptoms promptly throughout follow-up. Quality-of-life questionnaires will be completed at baseline and weekly during follow-up, including the actual Final Visit. Oura-derived measures will be collected from screening through the actual Final Visit. PsyTool assessments and other exploratory measures will be collected at different timepoints.

After the individual Final Visit or Early Termination Visit, safety information received during six months of passive follow-up will be assessed. This period adds no scheduled study visits, routine diary entries, questionnaires or biomarker samples. The Investigator may arrange additional care or assessments when clinically indicated.

The primary purpose is safety and tolerability assessment. Without a concurrent control group, exploratory changes may reflect natural variability, practice effects, concomitant factors or expectation effects. They will be interpreted as hypothesis-generating observations.

abstract: The clinical translation of mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (mRNA-LNP) therapeutics is constrained by limited stability of liquid formulations, necessitating ultra-cold storage and restricting global accessibility. Here, we report a spray-dried dry powder platform for mRNA-LNPs that overcomes these limitations while enabling flexible routes of administration. Systematic evaluation of pharmaceutically relevant sugars identifies trehalose as an optimal matrix former, yielding high-recovery mRNA-LNP dry powder product (DPP) with controlled particle size, low residual moisture, and preserved LNP physicochemical properties upon reconstitution. Mechanistic studies combining solid-state characterization, fluorescence tracking, and solvent extraction demonstrate that mRNA-LNPs are entrapped within an amorphous trehalose matrix core, providing protection against dehydration and rehydration stress. Reconstituted DPP (RDPP) maintains in vivo protein expression comparable to liquid control (LC) following intravenous and intramuscular administration, while supporting effective mucosal delivery via pulmonary and sublingual routes. Direct administration of DPP without reconstitution enables lung-targeted protein expression, highlighting potential for cold-chain-independent therapies. Critically, DPP preserves colloidal stability, mRNA integrity, ionizable lipid stability, and biological activity for over 3 years under refrigerated conditions, whereas liquid formulation exhibits substantial degradation within 6-9 months. These findings establish spray-dried mRNA-LNP DPPs as a robust platform integrating long-term stability with multi-route delivery for improved accessibility of mRNA therapeutics.

abstract: Efficient engineering of human and murine primary T cells without perturbation of cellular function is crucial for immunotherapy and immunology research. Here, we present a protocol for genome editing of primary T cells with minimal toxicity using peptide-assisted genome editing. We describe key steps required for primary T cell isolation and activation, CRISPR ribonucleoprotein (RNP) assembly and delivery mediated by peptide, and assessment of editing efficiency. This protocol maintains T cell proliferative capacity and functional potency. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Zhang et al.1.

description:
Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality globally, with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounting for approximately 85% of all diagnoses. For patients with metastatic NSCLC lacking actionable driver mutations (e.g., EGFR, ALK), the standard first-line therapeutic strategy involves immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) targeting the programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) or programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) axis, administered either as monotherapy or in combination with platinum-doublet chemotherapy. While these regimens have significantly improved overall survival (OS), a substantial proportion of patients fail to derive durable clinical benefit, and long-term survival rates for metastatic disease remain suboptimal, often due to host-related factors that impair the anti-tumor immune response.

A critical determinant of poor therapeutic outcomes in advanced NSCLC is cancer-associated cachexia (CAC), a multifactorial paraneoplastic syndrome characterized by systemic inflammation, negative protein-energy balance, and the involuntary loss of skeletal muscle mass (sarcopenia). Primary observational studies demonstrate that nutritional derangements closely associated with cachexia - such as significant weight loss and malnutrition - are highly prevalent in lung cancer, particularly in advanced disease, with lung cancer-specific cohorts reporting rates ranging from approximately 35% - 70% depending on disease stage and assessment method. Unlike starvation, it is driven by aberrant systemic inflammation and not fully reversible via nutritional support.

Clinically, cachexia is defined by the international consensus (Fearon criteria) as weight loss \>5% over 6 months, or weight loss \>2% in individuals with a body mass index (BMI) \< 20 kilograms per square meter (kg/m2) or sarcopenia. Sarcopenia is specifically defined by a low skeletal muscle index (SMI) at the L3 vertebral level, with widely validated cutoffs of \< 52.4 cm2/m2 for men and \< 8.5 cm2/m2 for women.

This is a Phase 1b/2, multi-site, single-arm, open-label, non-randomized study looking at whether adding tocilizumab to standard treatment for metastatic Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) is safe, possible, and effective. The study includes people with metastatic NSCLC, that is lung cancer that has spread, who have experienced significant loss of weight or muscle mass.

Primary Objective Evaluate the safety/feasibility and efficacy of adding tocilizumab to standard first-line chemo-immunotherapy in biomarker-selected patients with stage IV NSCLC, defined by weight loss ≥5% within the prior 6 months, or ≥2% if BMI \< 20 kilograms per square meter (kg/m2).

Co-primary endpoint 1: Safety/Feasibility Proportion of patients completing four cycles of chemo-IO + tocilizumab without grade ≥3 autoimmune or non-hematological treatment-related adverse events (TRAE). Feasibility will be defined as ≥80% completion; unacceptable toxicity as \>30% incidence of grade ≥3 serious AEs.

Co-primary endpoint 2: Progression-Free Survival Rate at 6 months Proportion of patients alive and progression-free at 6 months after starting therapy per RECIST v1.1, estimated by Kaplan-Meier and presented with a 95% CI.

Secondary Objectives Assess the effect of tocilizumab on body composition, inflammatory biomarkers, and treatment response.

Secondary Endpoints: change in weight/muscle mass (CT-based sarcopenia/Fearon index); Overall Response Rate (ORR); median Overall Survival Rate; and CRP levels from baseline to end of treatment.

Correlative Objectives Evaluate associations between treatment response (PFS rate at 6 months, ORR) and baseline inflammatory biomarkers (CRP) as well as molecular biomarkers (KRAS, STK11) identified by next-generation sequencing (NGS) of tumor tissue.

Exploratory Objectives Identify associations between treatment response (PFS rate at 6 months, ORR) and longitudinal measurements of CRP, IL-6, Cyclin D1 and Bcl-xL mRNA, as well as baseline PTPRT methylation.

Participants will go through the screening and baseline process to assess eligibility. If eligible, participants will attend study treatment visits every 21 days for about 3 months, an End of Treatment (EOT) visit about 30 days after the last dose of treatment, and follow up for up to 12 months after the EOT visit. Tocilizumab will be administered in addition to standard treatment regimens for NSCLC, at a dose of 8 mg/kg intravenous (IV) once every three weeks (once every 21 days); on day one of each treatment cycle. Tocilizumab is administered as a single IV drip infusion over 1 hour; it cannot be administered as bolus or push. Tocilizumab will be given for 4 doses, at the beginning of treatment, or until disease progression or unacceptable toxicities.

The study will be open at 4 VA hospitals, and planned enrollment is about 43 participants in total with about 11 participants from each site. This research study is expected to take about 4 years. Individual participation in the study will take about 18 months.

abstract: Antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) remain underexplored relative to siRNA and mRNA LNPs. Using an orthogonal workflow (DLS, NTA, AF4), we show that ionisable lipid identity and microfluidic flow rate govern key LNP attributes. Replacing SM-102 with MC3 increased size and reduced ASO recovery, while lower flow rates increased LNP size and improved recovery, highlighting formulation-property relationships for ASO LNP optimisation.

abstract: Live-cell nuclear imaging continues to be limited by the number of fluorescent moieties that may be recruited to the DNA locus of interest. Major advances in dCas9-based live-cell imaging have been made using plasmid-based expression systems that integrate many protein fluorophores into the dCas9 fluorescent ribonucleoprotein (fRNP) complex to increase the visibility of the resulting DNA labels. The dependence on exogenous DNA plasmids, however, precludes these strategies from applications where precise control of fRNP presence is necessary or possible plasmid integration into the genome is unacceptable. In this study, we evaluated the capacity for fluorescent guide RNA (gRNA) to improve the visibility of cellular DNA labels during live-cell imaging, bypassing the need for complex fluorescent protein expression and foreign DNA plasmid delivery. Both CRISPR RNA (crRNA) and trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA) components of the gRNA were modified with terminal cyanine 3 (Cy3) fluorophores before assembly into fRNP, and the impact on the brightness and signal-to-background (SNB) of the resulting DNA labels was evaluated at two different genomic loci: a repeat-rich Chr3 locus and chromosome telomeres. We further explored the visibility of DNA labeled with a "split" fRNP constructed from two individual tracrRNA fragments, rather than the complete 86 nt tracrRNA sequence, in order to reduce the costs and turnaround time of tracrRNA synthesis and to increase the terminal ends available for fluorophore modification. The 86 nt tracrRNA configuration bearing two terminal Cy3 modifications to both the crRNA and tracrRNA resulted in the greatest improvement to label visibility with a 190% increase in brightness and a 60% increase in SNB for both loci, on average, in comparison to the previously published fRNP containing only one Cy3 on the crRNA. The split tracrRNA fRNP was capable of labeling both genomic loci with varying success, imparting a maximum brightness improvement of 153% and an SNB improvement of 49% to Chr3 labeling, however, with no significant gains to brightness and 41% improved SNB for telomeres. For both the designs, label visibility improved consistently with additional fluorescence modification of the gRNA, indicating that the modifications were well tolerated, and further enhancement of gRNA fluorescence may continue to improve label visibility during live-cell imaging.

description: The investigators aim to test the activity of nivolumab monotherapy in primary breast tumors in a pre-operative window of opportunity trial. As the data of the investigators generated in the TONIC trial (metastatic TNBC) indicate that low dose doxorubicin may 'prime' the tumor microenvironment (TME) resulting in higher response rates on nivolumab, in addition, cohorts for treatment with nivolumab plus low dose doxorubicin will be opened. Given the emerging data on other immunomodulatory strategies, this platform study allows opening additional cohorts for promising novel immune-oncology (IO) drugs for which a strong efficacy signal has been seen without drug safety issues. The investigators will study the TME and systemic host factors with specific emphasis on immunosuppressive processes that can potentially be targeted by novel IO agents to further optimize BC immunotherapy.

abstract:
This study is researching an investigational drug, ALN-HSD called "study drug". This study is focused on participants who are known to have Metabolic dysfunction-Associated SteatoHepatitis (MASH). MASH is a form of Metabolic dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MASLD). MASH occurs when fat builds up in liver cells, damaging them, and making the liver inflamed and stiff from fibrosis (scar tissue). MASH can progress to cirrhosis (long term scarring) and liver failure (when the liver cannot perform its job). The aim of the study is to see the effect of the study drug on lessening liver scarring related to MASH.

The study is looking at several other research questions, including:

* How ALN-HSD works to improve liver function and lessen MASH-related inflammation in the liver
* What side effects may happen from receiving the study drug
* How much study drug and study drug metabolites (byproduct of the body breaking down the study drug) are in the blood at different times
* Better understanding of the study drug and MASH

abstract:
This study will test a Regeneron study drug called ALN-CIDEB to find out whether it may help treat a liver disease called alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD). ALD is a type of liver disease caused by drinking alcohol at levels that are harmful to the body. The study will also test ALN-CIDEB in participants who are known to have metabolic dysfunction- and alcohol- associated liver disease (MetALD), a subgroup of people that have features of both ALD and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).

The study will compare 2 different dose regimens of ALN-CIDEB with placebo (something that looks like the study drug but doesn't contain any medicine) to understand how well ALN-CIDEB works to lower the amount of fat in the liver.

The study is looking at:

* What side effects ALN-CIDEB might cause
* How well ALN-CIDEB works to change liver fat and stiffness of the liver
* How ALN-CIDEB could affect the liver proteins

abstract: This phase 1 study will evaluate the safety, tolerability, and immune responses of two experimental mRNA HIV vaccines in adults living with HIV who are in overall good health. The study will enroll about 42 participants at multiple study sites. Researchers will assess whether these vaccines can start or strengthen antibody responses against HIV. The study will also evaluate how a closely monitored planned pause in antiretroviral therapy affects these immune responses.

abstract: Oligonucleotide therapeutics have emerged as next-generation therapeutics. However, targeted delivery of oligonucleotides to extrahepatic tissues, such as skeletal and cardiac muscles and the central nervous system, at efficacious yet well-tolerated doses remain a major challenge for their clinical translation. Although antibody-oligonucleotide conjugates are promising for the treatment of genetic disorders, inadequate tissue penetration and immunogenicity have constrained their therapeutic efficacy. By combining the advantages of cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) or cell-targeting peptides (CTPs) with those of oligonucleotides, peptide-oligonucleotide conjugates (POCs) display enhanced cellular uptake, endosomal escape, and extrahepatic delivery. The therapeutic efficacy of POC was increased through conjugation with CPPs, endosomal-escape peptides (EEPs), fusogenic peptides, nuclear localization signal peptides, or CTPs. In this perspective, innovative molecular designs such as multivalent, cyclic, and chimeric peptides, and combinations of CPPs and EEPs, were explored, highlighting key advancements in POC development and providing insights into future directions for the development of novel POCs.

Study details include:

* The study duration will be approximately 3 months per participant.
* Study intervention will be administered via a single intramuscular (IM) injection into the deltoid muscle on Day 1.
* The visit frequency will be Day 1, Day 9 telephone call, Day 29, and Day 91 telephone call (3-month safety follow-up).

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are a leading platform for nucleic acid delivery, yet current formulations typically suffer from rapid in vivo clearance and limited extrahepatic delivery. Recent experiments demonstrate that increasing the helper lipid content (e.g., to 40% 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine [DSPC]) can significantly improve mRNA stability, prolong circulation, and enhance transfection efficiency. In this study, we used coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to provide mechanistic insight into the structural changes driving these improvements. Our simulations confirm that an elevated helper lipid content fundamentally alters the internal morphology of the LNP. Consistent with experimental observations, at high DSPC levels, the core transitions from a compact, disordered, predominantly lipid state to an extended structure with distinct lamellar-like elements encompassing lipid-rich and water-rich regions. This structural reorganization can be used to rationalize the enhanced stability and delivery properties reported in the experiments. These findings provide a molecular-level understanding of the composition-morphology relationship and suggest that coarse-grained modeling can inform the design of novel LNP formulations.

abstract: Although cancer immunotherapy has revolutionized cancer therapy, the clinical efficacy of this approach is restricted due to tumor heterogeneity, immune escape, therapeutic resistance, poor tumor penetration, and toxic side effects. Short single-stranded DNA or RNA oligonucleotides, termed aptamers, have high affinity for a given target, low immunogenicity, and high chemical programmability and are emerging as promising agents for precision cancer therapies and immuno-oncology. This review aims to provide a comprehensive, integrated overview of the development of aptamer-based cancer therapeutics, from molecular engineering and pharmacology to clinical applications and translational potential. The discovery and optimization of tumor and immune-specific aptamers have been enhanced by the development of conventional SELEX, Cell-SELEX, in vivo SELEX, high-throughput sequencing, microfluidic selection, and AI-assisted selection. To enhance nuclease resistance, circulation time, biodistribution, and tumor accumulation, chemical modifications such as PEGylation, 2'-fluoro, 2'-O-methyl, LNAs, phosphorothioate linkages, circularization, and lipid/albumin binding have been developed. Aptamers can directly regulate oncogenic and immune signaling pathways or be used as targeted delivery vehicles for chemotherapeutic drugs, siRNAs, miRNAs, proteins, peptides, and CRISPR-based systems. Moreover, aptamers targeting tumor-associated biomarkers, cancer stem cells, the tumor vasculature, stromal components, and immune regulatory pathways have the potential to selectively remodel the tumor microenvironment. In addition, they are well-suited to other immunotherapy strategies, including immune checkpoint inhibitors, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, photodynamic or photothermal therapy, oncolytic viruses, and cancer vaccines, thereby further supporting a multifunctional, personalized treatment approach. Although there has been significant progress in pre-clinical research, several issues remain regarding pharmacokinetics, tumor penetration, off-target effects, manufacturing, long-term safety, regulatory approval, and clinical validation. Additional advancements in aptamer engineering, nanotechnology, computational design, and biomarker-directed therapy could potentially enable the development of these platforms into successful next-generation precision cancer immunotherapies.

abstract: Gliomas are increasingly recognized as network diseases in which aberrant interactions between tumor cells, neurons, and immune populations drive hyperexcitability, seizures, cognitive dysfunction, and disease progression. Simultaneously, advances in structural biology and nucleic acid engineering have revealed DNA to be a dynamic molecular architecture capable of sensing, regulating, and modulating cellular states. In this review, we examine how noncanonical DNA structures and functional nucleic acids including Z-DNA, G-quadruplexes, cruciform structures, aptamers, and DNA origami systems, shape neural regulation and glioma associated circuit pathology. We discuss how activity dependent DNA conformational transitions influence transcriptional programs controlling neurotransmission, ion channel expression, synaptic signaling, metabolism, and inflammatory pathways in glioma cells and peritumoral neural networks. Z-DNA formation appears linked to rapid transcriptional activation and enhancer dynamics, whereas G-quadruplex rich regulatory regions modulate genes associated with excitatory signaling, cellular proliferation, and tumor progression. Cruciform DNA structures additionally interface with genome stability and DNA repair, creating mechanistic entry points for therapeutic intervention. Beyond endogenous DNA architectures, we highlight the emergence of aptamer based diagnostics and therapeutics capable of detecting neurotransmitters, cytokines, and metabolites associated with glioma induced network dysfunction. DNA origami platforms further enable programmable multivalent delivery systems for targeted transport of small molecules, oligonucleotides, CRISPR machinery, and ion-channel modulators across the neurovascular unit and tumor microenvironment. We also explore closed-loop neuromodulatory strategies in which electrophysiological signatures guide state dependent therapeutic actuation through nucleic acid based sensing and delivery systems. Finally, we discuss key translational considerations, including blood brain barrier delivery, nuclease stability, immunogenicity, biodistribution, manufacturing reproducibility, and integration with existing neuro-oncology and anti-seizure therapies. By bridging molecular origami, electrophysiology, and neurotechnology, this review proposes a framework for precision neuromedicine in glioma and broader neurological disease, where programmable nucleic acid architectures are coupled to the dynamic circuit states that drive pathology.

abstract: The transcription factor (TF) SPI1 (historically called PU.1) is a critical pioneer TF and regulator of hematopoiesis. It exerts exquisitely dose-dependent and stage-specific control over lymphoid, myeloid, and central nervous system-resident lineages. Structurally characterized by an intrinsically disordered N-terminal transactivation region and a highly conserved C-terminal DNA-binding E26 transformation-specific domain, SPI1 can operate alone as a monomer, via homodimerization, through epigenetic interactions, and in context-dependent transcriptional partnerships. While early animal models established its essentiality for leukopoiesis, modern human genomics has unveiled direct links between altered SPI1 function and disease. Heterozygous loss-of-function germline variants cause PU.1-mediated agammaglobulinemia, whereas somatic mutations and/or regulatory alterations can drive hematologic malignancies. Dysregulated SPI1 activity is also implicated in autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus, and neurodegenerative disorders. This review reconciles foundational murine paradigms with emerging human translational data, highlights current therapeutic landscapes, and projects how single-cell multi-omics and advanced gene editing may shape future directions in the SPI1 biomedical field.

abstract:
This multi-site study will test whether an opportunistic AI-based CAC screening and notification intervention can improve cholesterol treatment and lower cholesterol levels in adults. The study uses artificial intelligence to detect calcium buildup in heart arteries (coronary artery calcium or CAC) on chest CT scans that patients have already had for other reasons. The study will focus on adults who either have known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) or have significant calcium buildup (a CAC score of 100 or higher), and whose cholesterol is not well controlled.

It will also evaluate how well this approach can be implemented at scale across multiple health systems. The main questions it aims to answer are:

Does notifying patients and their clinicians about incidental CAC increase lipid-lowering therapy(LLT) initiation or intensification?

Does the intervention improve Low-Density Lipoprotein(LDL)-cholesterol control and related lipid testing?

How does the intervention affect downstream care (e.g., clinic visits, cardiology referrals, and cardiac testing)?

Researchers will use an FDA-cleared AI algorithm to quantify CAC on previously performed non-gated chest CT scans and identify eligible participants through the electronic health record. Participants will be randomized to receive CAC notification either right away or after a 6-month delay.

abstract: The maintenance of blood homeostasis relies heavily on hematopoietic stem cells (HSC), whose function is highly sensitive to oxidative stress caused by disrupted equilibrium between reactive oxygen species (ROS) and antioxidant systems. This review provides a comprehensive examination of the current strategies aimed at therapeutically targeting oxidative stress in HSC, outlining both the challenges and the advancements in this domain. We discuss the intricate mechanisms by which oxidative stress disrupts HSC self-renewal, quiescence, and differentiation, as well as the implications for aging and hematological malignancies. The function of the hypoxic bone marrow microenvironment in reducing oxidative damage is highlighted alongside the metabolic adaptations that support HSC viability. Furthermore, we explore emerging therapeutic approaches, including antioxidants, gene editing technologies, and niche modulation, that aim to enhance HSC function and resilience in the face of oxidative stress. Drawing on recent preclinical and clinical findings, this review highlights the need for novel strategies that integrate a deeper understanding of redox biology with therapeutic interventions to enhance outcomes in HSC transplantation and regeneration. This integration of current findings and emerging strategies provides valuable insights for developing targeted therapies aimed at preserving HSC integrity in the treatment of hematologic diseases.

title: Therapeutic Targeting of Oxidative Stress in Hematopoietic Stem Cells: Current Strategies and Future Directions.

abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Cryptococcus gattii ( C. gattii) is a pathogenic respiratory fungus that rapidly disseminates through the central nervous system. The current clinical treatments for C. gattii infections are limited by prolonged therapeutic courses, high drug dosages, and insufficient antifungal options. This study aimed to explore the molecular mechanisms underlying amphotericin B (AmB) resistance in C. gattii and provide novel insights for developing targeted antifungal strategies.
METHODS: A total of 27 clinical C. gattii isolates were subjected to antifungal susceptibility testing, multilocus sequence typing (MLST) for phylogenetic analysis and resistance-related mutation screening. The CRISPR/Cas9 system was used to construct an SSK2-knockout mutant ( ssk2Δ-G4). Capsule and melanin assays, murine pulmonary infection models, and transcriptomic analyses were performed to verify gene function, evaluate therapeutic efficacy, and explore the underlying regulatory mechanisms.
RESULTS: G4 isolates exhibited prominent AmB resistance with a novel SSK2 c.793A>G missense mutation (p.Thr265Ala; hereafter SSK2 T265A). SSK2 knockout significantly enhanced AmB susceptibility, whereas SSK2 T265A complementation partially restored the resistant phenotype. AmB treatment markedly reduced pulmonary fungal burden and inflammatory infiltration ( P < 0.05) and improved survival ( P < 0.001) in ssk2Δ-G4-infected mice. Mechanistically, this mutation upregulated CAT1 expression and enhanced the reactive oxygen species-scavenging capacity and oxidative stress tolerance.
CONCLUSION: SSK2 c.793A>G is closely associated with AmB resistance and functionally contributes to the resistance phenotype. SSK2 could serve as a potential therapeutic target for developing AmB synergistic sensitizers and as a research direction for future synergistic treatments of clinically resistant C. gattii strains.

abstract: The global antimicrobial resistance crisis, driven primarily by the ESKAPE pathogen consortium has catalyzed the translation of engineered bacteriophage therapeutics from experimental platforms to clinical-stage precision medicines. Unlike their wild-type counterparts, which are constrained by narrow host ranges, susceptibility to reticuloendothelial clearance, and limited biofilm penetrability, synthetically engineered phages exploit receptor-binding protein remodeling, phage-derived enzymatic depolymerases, CRISPR-Cas3 chromosomal shredding payloads, sequence-independent SASPject delivery vectors, and in vivo microbiome base editors to overcome the multilayered resistance arsenals of MDR ESKAPE organisms. Recent clinical development has generated human evidence across both genetically engineered phage platforms and advanced fixed phage-cocktails. Engineered programmes include CRISPR-Cas3-based LBP-EC01 and SNIPR001, while AP-SA02 represents an analytically characterized fixed multi-phage cocktail targeting Staphylococcus aureus. This review examines engineering strategies, pharmacokinetics, immune-mediated clearance, delivery challenges, clinical evidence, manufacturing, and regulatory pathways. It also discusses emerging regulatory approaches and distinctions between natural and genetically modified phage products. The literature search was conducted from January-June 2026 using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, supplemented by searches of ClinicalTrials.gov and the websites of the US-FDA and EMA. Overall, this review evaluates the translational potential of engineered phages, identifies barriers to clinical adoption, and considers future developments in precision antimicrobial therapy against multidrug-resistant pathogens.

title: Engineered bacteriophages as precision antimicrobials against multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens: molecular engineering strategies, clinical translation, and the crystallizing global regulatory landscape.

abstract: Hyperlipidemia is a systemic metabolic disorder closely associated with chronic inflammation. Effective management requires integrated strategies that simultaneously lower lipid level and attenuate inflammation. Nucleic acid therapeutics, such as proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) siRNA, represent a breakthrough in lipid-lowering therapy. However, they either lack direct anti-inflammatory effects (GalNAc-siRNA) or are prone to triggering unintended inflammatory responses themselves such as lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). Milk-derived extracellular vesicles (MDEs) emerge as naturally anti-inflammatory nanocarriers that suppress key pro-inflammatory cytokines by 30.0%-96.5% in vitro. However, MDEs predominantly undergo endocytic trafficking with substantial endosomal/lysosomal sequestration, which can limit productive cytosolic siRNA delivery. To address this, we developed engineered MDEs by incorporating 30.0% (w/w) probiotic-derived glycolipids into their membranes to facilitate early endosomal escape. When loaded with PCSK9 siRNA, the engineered MDEs achieved a remarkable silencing efficiency of 90.2 ± 0.2%, significantly outperforming both unmodified MDEs and conventional LNPs. In hyperlipidemic mice, systemic administration of engineered MDEs improved serum lipid profiles, reduced lipid accumulation and systemic inflammation, and showed a favorable safety profile under the conditions examined. Collectively, this work provides a promising nucleic acid delivery platform based on engineered MDEs for enhanced hyperlipidemia therapy through simultaneous lipid-lowering and anti-inflammatory effects.

abstract: Osteosarcoma is a highly aggressive primary bone malignancy characterized by rapid proliferation, chemoresistance, and early metastasis. Recent advances in CRISPR/Cas (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats/CRISPR-associated proteins) genome editing have enabled precise targeting of oncogenes, tumor suppressors, and regulators of epigenetic, metabolic, and signaling pathways, providing new insights into osteosarcoma biology. CRISPR-mediated knockout of cell-cycle regulators, including CDK11, impairs proliferation, while restoration of TP53 and suppression of TERT promoter activity inhibits tumor growth. Other line of studies has revealed that chemoresistance mechanisms mediated by ABCB1/MDR1, CD44, ATR, RAD18, and autophagy-related genes have been effectively reversed through CRISPR interventions, restoring sensitivity to cisplatin and doxorubicin. Furthermore, CRISPR applications in immune modulation, such as PD-L1 knockout, may enhance antitumor immunity. Importantly, high-throughput CRISPR screens also may identify essential genes, novel oncogenic drivers, and synthetic lethal targets, thus informing potential precision therapeutic strategies. This review aims to critically summarize CRISPR/Cas-mediated studies in osteosarcoma, focusing on targeting oncogenes and tumor suppressors, overcoming chemoresistance, modulating immune responses, regulating metabolism and autophagy, and identifying essential genes and vulnerabilities, providing a translational framework for precision therapy.

abstract: Newcastle disease virus (NDV or AOaV-1) is an avian paramyxovirus that typically causes only mild, self-limiting disease in humans. Here, we report fatal neuroinvasive AOaV-1 infection in a patient with multiple myeloma receiving maintenance therapy with teclistamab, daratumumab, and lenalidomide following frontline teclistamab-based treatment and autologous stem cell transplantation. Following rapidly progressive brainstem-cerebellar encephalitis and negative conventional microbiological testing, unbiased metagenomic RNA sequencing of a cerebellar biopsy identified AOaV-1 at high intraparenchymal abundance. Viral genome analysis revealed striking A-to-G and U-to-C substitutions selectively concentrated in the matrix gene, consistent with ADAR-mediated RNA editing. Long-read sequencing resolved two genetically distinct, independently hypermutated CNS haplotypes. Post-mortem analysis demonstrated widespread dissemination and continued viral diversification in multiple brain regions, whereas a peripheral urine sample contained a minimally mutated putative ancestral lineage. These findings support peripheral infection followed by CNS seeding and compartmentalized within-host evolution. The selective matrix-gene hypermutation closely parallels persistent measles virus infection in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, revealing a shared mechanism of paramyxovirus adaptation to the CNS. Profound immunotherapy-associated immune dysfunction may thus create niches enabling normally low-pathogenic zoonotic viruses to persist, evolve, and acquire severe neurovirulence.

abstract: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats -Artificial Intelligence (CRISPR-AI) convergence generate therapeutic candidates via iterative human-machine workflows that disrupt the inventorship criterion of patent law based on conception. In CRISPR-AI studies, AI systems suggest thousands of guide RNAs or Cas variants; human researchers select, confirm, and optimize them via experimental feedback loops that conceal the locus of conception. The existing patent doctrine, which demands a clear and final concept in the human mind, fails to align with inventions in which AI comes up with solutions that human researchers had not anticipated. This Article advances a recognition pathway for CRISPR-AI inventorship that maintains the natural-person baseline while attributing inventorship to humans who exercise claim-defining technical judgment in identifying patentable value within AI outputs. The Article reconceives the person having ordinary skill in the art standard for AI-enhanced biotechnology, rejecting both inflexible pre-AI baselines and the 'computer having ordinary skill in the art' proposal. A five-factor test is employed to assess AI-generated CRISPR inventions on non-obviousness in terms of problem structure, predictability of solutions, and quality of human judgment. The framework provides a computational biotechnology human-accountability grammar that is administrable, but not legally granted to machines.

title: The recognition pathway: reconceiving inventorship and obviousness for iterative CRISPR-AI convergence.

abstract: Pigs and chickens are not only the most important livestock species for global food production but also serve as key model organisms in various research disciplines. The pig is widely used in translational research due to its anatomical and physiological similarity to humans, providing valuable insights into immunology, metabolism, and disease mechanisms. In contrast, the chicken has become an essential model for studies related to poultry health, animal welfare, and developmental biology. Its externally developing embryo offers exceptional accessibility for experimental manipulation. Recent advances in genome editing technologies, particularly CRISPR/Cas9, have further expanded the potential of these species for functional genomic studies, although the efficient delivery of such tools remains a major challenge. Here, we overcome this delivery limitation by using virus-like particles (VLPs). We evaluated VLPs as delivery vehicles for genome engineering tools in porcine and avian cultures, two key livestock species at the human-animal interface. VLP-mediated delivery enabled efficient Cre recombination and high CRISPR/Cas9 editing rates in porcine cells, organoids, and oocytes, particularly when multiplexed. In chickens, VLPs supported robust Cre recombination and Cas9-mediated editing in cell culture, tracheal organ cultures, and in ovo. Reporter VLPs and dCas9 VLPs further demonstrated the versatility of this platform across porcine and avian systems. Together, these findings establish VLPs as an efficient and time-saving strategy for gene editing in livestock cultures across in vitro, ex vivo and in ovo systems, with potential future applications for animal health, agricultural productivity, and translational One Health research.

abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are essential for neuronal development and brain function. We investigated the role of a recurrent AMPAR GluA1 variant (GRIA1 p.A636T) identified in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using a Gria1-A636T knock-in mouse model, we show that this variant is sufficient to produce core ASD/ID-like behaviors and cause selective hippocampal vulnerability characterized by progressive dendritic atrophy and neuronal loss. Despite a reduction in GluA1-containing complexes, synaptic AMPARs exhibit hyperexcitability and fail to transition from calcium-permeable to calcium-impermeable AMPARs during development, resulting in persistent excitotoxicity. To explore potential therapeutic interventions, we developed an allele-specific antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) to selectively silence the mutant transcript. A single neonatal ASO dose prevents hippocampal pathology and rescues behavioral deficits. These findings define a mechanism of developmental excitotoxicity driven by a GRIA1 gain-of-function channelopathy and support RNA-targeted precision therapy for AMPAR-related neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Antisense oligonucleotide silencing rescues neurodevelopmental deficits in AMPA receptor gain-of-function mice.

abstract: Impaired expression of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) greatly compromises cytotoxic T-cell-mediated anticancer immunotherapy. Existing MHC-I activation strategies are greatly challenged by poor tumor specificity and off-target toxicity. Herein, we report a dual tumor-specific CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system that can precisely knock out succinate dehydrogenase subunit C (Sdhc) to activate the MHC-I pathway via epigenetic and transcriptional regulation. A tumor-specific gene editor is first engineered via reversible shielding of sgRNA using an apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (APE1)-responsive, complementary ssDNA, yielding AP-sgRNA with blocked editing activity in normal cells yet completely restored activity in APE1-overexpressing tumor cells. Subsequently, tumor-targeted delivery of AP-sgRNA and Cas9 mRNA (mCas9) is achieved using dibenzocyclooctyne-decorated lipid nanoparticle (DLNP), which upon bioorthogonal click reaction can anchor cancer cells that are prelabeled with azido groups using the unnatural sugar DCL-AAM. Thus, AP-sgSdhc/mCas9@DLNP enables efficient and selective Sdhc editing in tumor cells, leading to epigenetic and transcriptional activation of MHC-antigen processing and presentation genes and thereby provoking robust antitumor efficacy in the B16-OVA melanoma model through enhanced, T cell-mediated immune responses. Moreover, it completely suppressed pulmonary metastasis after combination with aPD-L1 in the 4T1 lung metastasis model. This study provides an enlightened paradigm for precision gene editing and renders a promising mechanism for potentiating cancer immunotherapy.

title: Tumor-Specific Gene Editing Enhances Cancer Immunogenicity through Succinate Metabolism-Mediated MHC-I Reprogramming.

abstract: Noncoding sequences comprise most of the human genome; however, their functional significance remains largely elusive. Using CRISPR tiling mutagenesis with near-PAMless, high-fidelity SpRY-Cas9, we mapped the fitness landscape of an entire human gene, the 10-kb MYC locus, at base-pair resolution. This unbiased interrogation revealed that 67% of functionally essential base pairs are noncoding. Essential noncoding base pairs are under strong constraint in the human population but show limited evolutionary conservation across species. Within this landscape, we identified an ultraconserved noncoding RNA element in the 3' untranslated region (UTR) that promotes perinuclear localization of MYC mRNA and nuclear localization of MYC protein through interaction with hnRNP L. Steric-blocking antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting this element selectively eliminate diverse MYC-dependent cancer cells and inhibit growth of patient-derived tumor organoids. Together, these findings establish noncoding sequences as major carriers of functional genetic information and identify a therapeutically actionable RNA element whose targeting disrupts MYC-driven cancer.

title: CRISPR mutagenesis of the MYC locus reveals a druggable ultraconserved RNA element.

abstract: Here, we present a CRISPR-Cas9 protocol for generating both small indels and multi-kilobase deletions to enable genome editing in human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). We describe steps for a ribonucleoprotein (RNP)-based approach that integrates guide RNA selection, electroporation, and multi-tiered screening to accurately identify indels, deletions, inversions, and mixed genotypes. Human iPSCs provide a versatile genome editing platform due to their capacity for clonal expansion and differentiation. This protocol provides a scalable framework for genome editing and quality control. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Hamerlinck et al.1.

title: CRISPR-based pipeline for generating and validating multi-kb deletions and indels in iPSCs.

abstract: RNA aptamers are short, single-stranded RNA molecules that fold into specific three-dimensional structures and selectively bind molecular targets. Despite applications in therapeutics, diagnostics, and biosensing, tools for aptamer validation remain scarce compared to well-established pipelines for other biomolecular binders such as antibodies. Here, we introduce SecAntiGami─a secondary-antibody-inspired RNA origami─as a modular tool for signal enhancement and aptamer characterization. SecAntiGami binds aptamers of interest through programmable kissing-loop interactions and carries a fluorescent aptamer for visualization. It amplifies aptamer-dependent size increases in dynamic light scattering assays and enables fluorescence-based aptamer localization. We rationally design three different variants of a biotin-binding aptamer and use SecAntiGami to demonstrate that all of them retain their functionality, enabling efficient integration of aptamers into RNA origami structures. SecAntiGami serves as a versatile tool for qualitative aptamer validation for synthetic biology, structural RNA nanotechnology, RNA therapeutics, and diagnostics.

title: SecAntiGami: A Secondary-Antibody-Inspired RNA Origami for Qualitative Aptamer Validation.

abstract: Filamentous fungi are important microbial cell factories for producing antibiotics, organic acids, enzymes, and other valuable products, with broad applications in food, agriculture, and medicine. However, inefficient and imprecise genome editing remains a major bottleneck limiting rational strain engineering. This review summarizes major genome-editing tools in filamentous fungi, including Cre-loxP, TALENs, and CRISPR-Cas systems, with emphasis on their mechanisms, advantages, and limitations. We highlight CRISPR-Cas9 as the predominant platform and discuss optimization strategies involving sgRNA design, engineered Cas9 variants, promoter engineering, AMA1-based replicative plasmids, and ribonucleoprotein delivery. Emerging technologies, including base editing, prime editing, Cas12a, and Mad7, are also discussed for their potential to broaden editing capabilities. Finally, we outline future perspectives focusing on extending the application of existing genome-editing systems in filamentous fungi and discovering novel genome-editing tools from large-scale omics data sets. This review will accelerate the development of filamentous fungi as versatile platforms for biomanufacturing.

title: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Palindromic Repeats-Cas Genome-Editing Systems in Filamentous Fungi: Current Tools, Optimization Strategies, and Future Perspectives.

abstract:
MOTIVATION: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) are critical to protein activity, yet the biological role of most known modification sites remains uncharacterized. CRISPR-mediated phenotypic screens using base editors offer a powerful approach to dissecting PTM function at scale. However, existing single-guide RNA (sgRNA) design tools for base editing applications are DNA-centric and lack the throughput required to integrate seamlessly with mass-spectrometry-based proteomics experimental outputs.
RESULTS: We introduce protein editing in R, PrEditR, an open-source, protein-centric tool for high-throughput sgRNA design for custom base editor screens. PrEditR enables users to designate specific amino acid residues in proteins and design protospacer sequences that target the corresponding gene and annotate every resulting amino acid change (missense, nonsense, or silent), including bystander edits.
AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: PrEditR is available on GitHub and Docker Hub.

abstract: Interface integration failure after implanting bone repair material is a core challenge in treating bone defects. This study aimed to investigate the molecular mechanism by which endothelial cell-derived small extracellular vesicles (EC-sEVs) deliver lncRNA DLX1 (lncDLX1) to regulate the osteogenic differentiation of BMSCs through both in vitro and in vivo experiments. The results showed that lncDLX1 expression was significantly downregulated in an inflammatory microenvironment and that overexpression of lncDLX1 promoted BMSC osteogenic differentiation while inhibiting inflammatory responses. Mechanistic studies revealed that lncDLX1 binds to RBMX, which then transcriptionally activates β-catenin expression and enhances its mRNA stability by binding to the CTNNB1 promoter region, thereby activating the Wnt/β-catenin pathway. Functional experiments confirmed that EC-sEVscould be effectively taken up by BMSCs and functionally deliver lncDLX1, and GW4869 treatment attenuated this regulatory effect, supporting the involvement of sEVs. In vivo experiments showed that hydroxyapatite materials loaded with lncDLX1-overexpressing BMSCs significantly promoted bone repair in a rat femoral defect model. In summary, this study reveals the central role of the EC-sEVs/lncDLX1/RBMX/Wnt/β-catenin signaling axis in bone repair, providing a new theoretical basis for the development of sEV-based lncRNA bone repair strategies.

abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a heterogeneous and aggressive hematologic malignancy associated with poor survival despite recent therapeutic advances. To identify novel anti-leukemic agents, we performed a high-throughput viability screen of 10,000 small molecules across 56 genetically diverse primary AML samples. Compounds with similar activity profiles were grouped into Compound Correlation Clusters (CCCs), leading to the identification of CCC163, which includes AML874, as a potent and selective hit. Integrated pharmacological and CRISPR-Cas9 approaches identified the Mediator complex as the molecular target of AML874. We demonstrated that AML874 acts as a selective CDK8/CDK19 inhibitor, disrupting Mediator-dependent transcription. FLT3-mutated AML showed increased sensitivity to AML874, suggesting a subtype-specific vulnerability. Notably, CDK8 inhibition synergized with venetoclax in AML cell lines and patient-derived xenograft models, resulting in enhanced anti-leukemic activity in vivo. Collectively, these findings establish CDK8/CDK19 inhibition as a therapeutically relevant strategy in AML.

title: Mediator kinase inhibition exposes a transcriptional vulnerability and synergizes with venetoclax in AML.

abstract: Activating mutations in PIK3CA (encoding the p110α kinase) are among the most frequent oncogenic drivers in human tumors. The two major hotspot mutations, E545K (helical domain) and H1047R (kinase domain), both hyperactivate PI3K-AKT signaling, yet they exhibit distinct functional behaviors and differential drug sensitivities. The mutation-specific protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks underlying the differences, however, remain largely unexplored. In this study, we established experimental approaches to identify proteins in proximity to oncogenic PI3K using biotin ligase-based proximity labeling. Our data revealed that the PIK3CA H1047R and E545K mutants fused to BioID2 formed structurally distinct complexes, each associating with unique proximal proteins identified by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Further integration of the PPI networks with CRISPR dependency screens and multiomic profiling mapped the divergent functional interactomes of p110α hotspot mutants. H1047R exhibited a synthetic lethal dependency on the adaptor protein TAB2, which is associated with aggressive clinical phenotypes in breast cancer. Distinctly, E545K interacted with core subunits of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex, corresponding to a globally repressive chromatin state at distal enhancers. This SWI/SNF association also revealed a mutation-specific epigenetic vulnerability, with E545K-mutant cells displaying increased sensitivity to EZH2 inhibitors. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the molecular network complexity of oncogenic PI3K can be interrogated through proximity labeling and that distinct PIK3CA point mutations rewire non-overlapping PPI networks, revealing domain-specific dependencies. Our study provides a framework for mapping mutation-specific interactomes and offers molecular insights and potential therapeutic strategies for PIK3CA-mutant tumors.

title: Integrative proximity labeling and multiomic profiling uncover domain-specific interactomes and molecular vulnerabilities of oncogenic PI3K.

abstract: Accurate detection of gene mutations is crucial for acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) diagnosis and treatment. Although CRISPR/Cas systems enable sensitive mutation detection, their adaptability is constrained by dependence on restriction endonucleases. Herein, we propose a two-step strategy, termed Fpg-RCA-CRISPR/Cas12a for ultrasensitive detection of the p53 R175H, which integrates formamidopyrimidine DNA glycosylase (Fpg)-mediated recognition with rolling circle amplification (RCA)-coupled CRISPR/Cas12a technology. Validation confirmed that Fpg exhibits minimal activity when adenine (A) is opposite the damaged site. Based on this finding, we designed a padlock probe with a site-specific 8-oxoguanine (8-oxoG) modification. This modification enables selective recognition of G > A mutations. For the target TP53 c.524G > A (p53 R175H), the G > A substitution opposite the 8-oxoG site blocks Fpg cleavage, facilitating probe circularization and subsequent RCA. The resulting RCA products then activate the trans-cleavage activity of Cas12a, enabling cascade signal amplification and generating a strong fluorescence output. For wild-type p53, Fpg-mediated cleavage prevents circularization and amplification, yielding weak fluorescence. Taking advantage of the high specificity of the Fpg enzyme and the cascade amplification effect of the RCA-CRISPR/Cas12a system, this method achieves a limit of detection (LOD) of 0.29 fM and covers a linear range from 0.8 fM to 800 pM, along with high reproducibility, excellent selectivity, and negligible background interference. Notably, the assay can detect mutation frequencies as low as 0.1% in excess wild-type p53. Crucially, its clinical feasibility was confirmed by analyzing human serum samples, yielding results consistent with standard assays and thus demonstrating its practical reliability and translational potential.

title: A Two-Step Strategy Based on Fpg Recognition and RCA-CRISPR/Cas12a for Ultrasensitive Detection of Gene Mutation.

abstract: Cell-surface proteins are important biomarkers for cell phenotyping, disease diagnosis, therapeutic evaluation, and drug screening. However, their quantitative analysis on intact living cells remains challenging because conventional methods often require cell lysis, fixation, repeated washing, extensive sample processing, or bulky instrumentation. Herein, we developed a modular and reconfigurable cell-surface-to-solution CRISPR-Cas12a platform for wash-free quantitative analysis of cell-surface proteins on intact living cells. Aptamer recognition of extracellularly accessible targets deblocks a DNA activator, thereby activating Cas12a trans-cleavage in solution and converting localized cell-surface recognition into amplified fluorescence while maintaining a low background in the absence of targets. Using EpCAM as a model target, we engineered a split dual-aptamer architecture that enabled cooperative target recognition, efficient activator deblocking, and low-background signal amplification. The platform achieved sensitive EpCAM detection with a limit of detection of 32 fM and enabled live-cell analysis down to 2 cells/μL. It distinguished cell populations with different surface EpCAM levels and quantitatively monitored epithelial-mesenchymal transition-associated changes in cell-surface EpCAM abundance. Coordinated redesign of the target-responsive nucleic acid components extended the platform to PTK7 detection and the analysis of drug-induced cell-surface PTK7 remodeling. Coupling the system to a lateral flow readout enabled portable visual detection. This work establishes a modular and reconfigurable CRISPR-Cas12a sensing strategy for wash-free amplified quantification of cell-surface proteins on living cells, providing a convenient tool for investigating their dynamic remodeling during physiological and pathological processes and therapeutic responses, as well as for drug screening.

title: Modular Cell-Surface-to-Solution CRISPR-Cas12a Platform for Wash-Free Quantification of Cell-Surface Proteins on Living Cells.

abstract: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis1. IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds to commensal microorganisms to regulate their colonization and function2,3, with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans, but difficult to study, because of its complex aetiology and comorbidities4-8. Here we use genetically and environmentally controlled mice to show that various models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to several models of endogenous colorectal cancer. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the structure of the antibody rather than to binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppressed epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein that is required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In IgA-knockout mice, deleting the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased epithelial cell proliferation and the increased tumour susceptibility seen in these mice. These experiments establish a homeostatic function for IgA in tempering physiological epithelial responses to the microbiota to maintain mucosal health.

abstract: The worldwide emergence of antimicrobial resistance and the need for non-conventional alternatives to conventional antibiotics have been increased by multidrug-resistant ESKAPE pathogens, which cause the majority of nosocomial infections and are starting to develop resistance to even the most potent drugs. Engineered bacteriophages are promising precision antimicrobials because of their ability to selectively infect and lyse bacterial hosts, multiply at infection sites, and co-evolve with bacterial populations to overcome resistance. Advances in synthetic biology, such as tail fiber modification, depolymerase and endolysin enhancement, genome editing using the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR), and computationally designed phage cocktails, have opened new possibilities for therapeutics that were hindered by the limitations of natural phages. These engineering strategies expand host range, enhance biofilm penetration, and target resistance genes. In spite of promising evidence in preclinical models, the use of engineered phages in routine clinical practice remains difficult. Specific key challenges include unclear regulations, lack of good manufacturing practice (GMP)grade production, variable pharmacokinetics and limited clinical trial data. This review critically examines engineering approaches to improve phage activity against ESKAPE pathogens, identifies the scientific and regulatory barriers limiting clinical use, and outlines the key steps needed for wider adoption.

abstract:
AIMS: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic β-cells. Although exogenous insulin remains the standard treatment, it does not restore physiological glucose regulation. Differentiation of human pluripotent stem cells into β-cells offers a scalable alternative to cadaveric islet transplantation and has progressed rapidly over the past decade, resulting in nine clinical trials at various stages of completion. Despite this progress, durable graft function remains constrained by two major challenges: the absence of key islet microenvironment components, such as vasculature, extracellular matrix and supporting cell types and continued vulnerability to autoimmune and alloimmune rejection.
METHODS & RESULTS: This review considers emerging technological approaches to overcome these barriers. Bioengineered niches, including multilineage organoids, functionalized hydrogels, decellularized matrices and bioprinting, aim to recreate the native islet microenvironment, while synthetic biology approaches, such as hypoimmune gene editing, CRISPR-based transcriptional control and stimulus-responsive survival circuits, seek to enhance grafts' resilience. Computational and single-cell approaches, including gene regulatory network analysis and digital twin frameworks, are beginning to provide predictive tools for benchmarking differentiation quality and forecasting graft outcomes.
CONCLUSION: Together, these complementary strategies, potentially tailored to individual patients, represent a realistic path towards safer, more effective and durable β-cell replacement therapies for type 1 diabetes.

abstract: Spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs), the primary auditory afferents in the inner ear, are vulnerable to degeneration from neuropathies, concussion, and aging, among other causes. Accurate quantification of SGNs is critical for assessing degeneration and therapeutic interventions, but manual counting is arduous due to dense cellular crowding and unreliable nuclear markers. Because SGNs receive input from GluA2-containing AMPA receptors, the transcripts for which must be RNA-edited for calcium impermeability, we hypothesized that SGNs express high levels of the RNA-editing enzyme ADARB1. Here, we confirm enriched expression of Adarb1 transcripts in SGNs and show that anti-ADARB1 antibodies robustly label the nuclei of type I and type II SGNs from young and aged mice, adult macaques, and adult humans. Neuronal versus glial specificity was confirmed using antibodies against neurofilament heavy chain (NFH), human antigen D (HuD), GATA binding protein 3 (GATA3), and SRY-box 2 (SOX2). A blinded investigator manually counted mouse SGNs via NFH, and these were compared to automated counts of ADARB1-positive nuclei using the analyze particles function in ImageJ. A concordance correlation coefficient and Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated strong agreement between the manual and automated counts. Together, these results suggest broad utility of ADARB1 immunolabeling for automated counts of SGNs across species.
